searchText: What may be missed here is the role profit switchers like nicehash play. If there are multiple competing coins to mine pre-merge you will see a lot more hashrate on profit switchers which makes the pre merge situation more dangerous as someone is able to quickly concentrate hashrate to attack. I fully expect someone to attempt an attack pre merge or at least to consider arranging one. So if there’s even a chance it should be eliminated. And not to throw flak on any single entity but there is a pool famous for its massive manipulation of crypto markets which also owns most of the asic farms that will suffer greatly from a merge. A side chain with a slowly increasing difficulty bomb to de-incentivize an attack is a great way to mitigate this risk but I think additional measures are needed as well to encourage decentralization of hashrate. Also I wanted to add that a side chain you can test new developments on may be attractive. I know one of the justifications for rolling out 1559 now is to test it on PoW. Eth is getting more centralized not less every month. Paying out miners for keep building the PoW chain after the merge and let difficulty bomb killing it seems to be a reasonable way, considering pay outs on the PoS chain. It shouldn't change the game significantly as rewards increase near the merge could do. And it uses a built-in mechanism (difficulty bomb) to stop mining. There are potential improvements of that strategy. Pay for empty blocks only and speed up difficulty bomb. But if we target difficulty bomb to make it near impossible to keep mining 3 months after the merge it could be enough. The questions are. Should those payments be made in a trustless way? How much of engineering efforts would it need to bring this trustless channel on? to clarify, the only reason to keep paying after the merge is to avoid the hashrate drop before the merge? Yes, paying after the merge creates a future value for miners which incentivises them to keep their hashpower in the network rather than selling the hardware or offering it on nicehash. Rewards ramp up near the merge is another way of creating future value. The problem is that it requires miners trust the developers, which isn't great in a game theoretic sense. Also, I think we need *way* more than 3 months to sufficiently mitigate the incentive breakage. Though, I *do* think we can reduce the block reward leading up to The Merge quite a bit to try to shed some hashing power so it isn't so expensive to properly incentivize miners. Hash rate dropping isn't the problem. It is that the incentive for miners to protect the network from attackers goes to 0 if rewards end at The Merge. Don't miners already trust the developers? Not really. They trust the fact that mining is required for the chain to continue to function (for now). Once The Merge happens, the developers could just remove any promised future ETH reward without miners having the power to do anything about it. got it, I considered this scenario as unrealistic I can very easily imagine demand from holders that the developers cut the reward going to miners who are just burning electricity. couldn't the developers also annul any rewards given to miners before the merge? It would require a hardfork which is not something easy to do but theoretically doable of course Miners would then just quit mining and Ethereum would halt. 🙂 The alternative is keep making profit and trust developers or don't trust anyone and quit, right? A promise of developers is a form of Proof-of-Authority solidified with a decent amount of engineering efforts spent on finding and implementing the solution. I feel like this is pretty strong to decide to make a quit despite of loosing potential profit what amount of time is on your mind? A social solution (e.g. an address funded by the EF with a public pronouncement that they will pay miners according to some schedule) is going to be faster and easier than a technical solution. And if only a portion of miners believe them that's better for those that remain, as they will gain from being a larger % of the post-merge hashpower. The amount required is more than I think any individual or organization will spend. It depends on how much security we need. We want to make it so attacking the network is non-profitable, even at the end. If 50% of the hashrate is worth $1B worth of ETH over the next 4 years, then the cost to holders of that hardware of burning Ethereum down is around $1B (assumes 4 year amortization of hardware). It could be a contract or EOA with pre-issued ETH, deployed at the merge HF Ah, you mean mint some money and give it to the EF to divvy out to miners? If 50% of hashrate is worth $1M worth of ETH over 4 years, then the cost to holders of that hardware of burning Etherceum down is around $1M. I feel like $1M is *way* too small. Given that you could make substantially more than that on ETH short positions, or double spending a $1M transfer to an exchange. This is probably the way to reduce the cost of hashrate. If rewards cut is done within enough amount of time prior the merge or gradually leading to the merge. yes Yeah, I do think we could reasonably shed some hashing power leading up to the merge, assuming the merge is far enough out to do so. Ethereum miners control a significant portion of the world's GPUs at the moment I believe, to the point where nVidia recently tried to brick GPU mining. If we drop rewards over the span of 3 months (for example) the shock to the global market I suspect will be too high to bear and we'll end up with a lot of mining hardware being rented out (and therefore useable in an attack). I very much dislike how speculative and intertangled all this is. 😢 I wish there was a solution that didn't require making guestimates all over the place. I think 4-year depreciation is reasonable, however the question is where that should start. I don't think it unreasonable to consider that point starting 3 years back, so a 1-year@2ETH/block->0ETH/block linear drop-off seems more than generous. 1 year from now 2 ETH -> 0 ETH? And yeah, there is a lot of guesswork involved. But I think it's one of those situations where ultimately picking something and sticking to it will be healthier than always searching for a better answer, because there will always be those who want to push for more or less, and with reasonable justification to do so. One option is to just *hope* that miners behave well after they don't have financial incentive to do so. 😬 From the merge (although i have no justification for my numbers it's just a thought as to how it could proceed) That is the extreme option, and the current default option. <dankrad> Here is an alternative: buy the GPUs after the merge <dankrad> Then we at least have the assets and aren't just burning money > If we drop rewards over the span of 3 months (for example) the shock to the global market I suspect will be too high to bear and we'll end up with a lot of mining hardware being rented out (and therefore useable in an attack). <dankrad> They could be useful for zero knowledge proofs To be clear, this would only be attacking other GPU PoW chains, not ethereum itself, right? As I don't think a 51% miner attack can actually do anything once the beacon chain takes over fork choice management I was thinking about buying hash power on nicehash if we see offers raising and targeting it back to ethereum 😆 Surely at nowhere near the scale of proof of work, though. <dankrad> No. But hash rate could drop enough before the merge to make attacks possible Hmm... having an emergency fund to purchase hash power if it looks like an attack is likely/occurring? Interesting idea Why would the hash rate drop before the mergE? I don't get this Of course no one would buy *new* hardware But existing hardware would surely keep running until the last day Assumedly if you know that at date x your hardware won't be able to make you money you either wait until time x and sell at the same time as everyone else in a depressed market, or get out a little bit ahead of everyone else. So when everyone tries the latter option you end up with a pre-emptive rush to the exit hmm that effect seems quite unlikely to take out a huge enough portion of hashpower to break things What if it won't drop but be offered via nicehash for much more money than it would get from keep mining next 100 blocks? (100 is an example) ah I see, because miners have no capital to defend at that point so they may as well just rent? yes, and someone could use it to attack sure so if we want the EF to fund a pool of exponentially increasing rewards for the last N blocks that go right up to the limit I'm fine with that What worries me about increased rewards is attracting more hashpower to the network which could neutralize the extra amount added to rewards. Though, it could be that much to buy all GPU hashpower on the market. Also, one another thing is that if for some reason we would have to postpone the merge (the emergency case) then those extra rewards will be paid to no purpose. The latter is unlikely, though, possible <dankrad> Why would it not be huge? In my mental model, it would drop very close to zero at merge (re @ef_general_chat_bridge_bot: <vbuterin> hmm that effect seems quite unlikely to take out a huge enough portion of hashpower to break things) <vbuterin> It feels really unlikely that everyone would try to sell proactively <vbuterin> My prediction is like 2/3 <vbuterin> Or even higher <vbuterin> Sorry I mean 2/3 of the hashpower will stay <adietrichs> Should the expecation of falling GPU prices not just lead to an approximate equilibrium where GPU prices slowly start to fall once we approach the merge? so basically where some time X before the merge the price is Y higher than immediately after the merge, where Y roughly accounts for the remaining profit to be expected from mining up to the merge? Seems to me it would end up with a relatively smooth (and relatively small) gradual hash rate reduction. (re @dankrad: Why would it not be huge? In my mental model, it would drop very close to zero at merge) <vbuterin> One good reason why it would not be very close to zero is that if that *was* true, at least some of whoever was *buying* the GPUs would see that there's an opportunity to temporarily run a piece of software and make a very huge chunk of money before moving back to what they wanted to do befoire as some miners start selling, the expected income for the remaining miners rises, doesn't it? <vbuterin> yes Yeah don't expect to see it all leaving, but is there then a danger that the GPU-based and lower-scale miners leave, and ends up with the majority of hashpower sitting with ASICs and large-scale operations (potentially only a handful of operations)? And do we care if that is the case? <vbuterin> hmm, not sure we need to care! <adietrichs> it might make sense to prepare for the case of a modification of the transition difficulty on short notice. that way we could always react to any unforseen problems. <adietrichs> like, once everyone is running combined clients, eth1 would listen to the first non-empty beacon application state anyway, correct? so the transition difficulty would only have to be adjusted on the eth2 side? could there be room for some sort of transition difficulty oracle setup? <vbuterin> hmm <vbuterin> If 51% attacks start happening, just telling eth2 clients to manually key in the transition application block hash seems reasonable <vbuterin> In which case the clients would need to include that as an option <n0ble> how could this case be identified? if difficulty on the canonical chain starts to drop off? (re @vbuterin: If 51% attacks start happening, just telling eth2 clients to manually key in the transition application block hash seems reasonable) <vbuterin> No, just if we see two long chains <adietrichs> would it make sense to loosen the validity rules around this then though? like, have eth2 blocks

What may be missed here is the role profit switchers like nicehash play. If there are multiple competing coins to mine pre-merge you will see a lot more hashrate on profit switchers which makes the pre merge situation more dangerous as someone is able to quickly concentrate hashrate to attack. I fully expect someone to attempt an attack pre merge or at least to consider arranging one. So if there’s even a chance it should be eliminated.

And not to throw flak on any single entity but there is a pool famous for its massive manipulation of crypto markets which also owns most of the asic farms that will suffer greatly from a merge.

Eth is getting more centralized not less every month.

excerpts.author: m.kalinin
excerpts.content:
Paying out miners for keep building the PoW chain after the merge and let difficulty bomb killing it seems to be a reasonable way, considering pay outs on the PoS chain. It shouldn't change the game significantly as rewards increase near the merge could do. And it uses a built-in mechanism (difficulty bomb) to stop mining.

There are potential improvements of that strategy. Pay for empty blocks only and speed up difficulty bomb. But if we target difficulty bomb to make it near impossible to keep mining 3 months after the merge it could be enough.

The questions are. Should those payments be made in a trustless way? How much of engineering efforts would it need to bring this trustless channel on?

excerpts.author: mheuer
excerpts.content:
I am a community member (and staker) and closely followed the discussion here.
I just want to point out the environmental impact if PoW is continued longer than necessary (https://digiconomist.net/ethereum-energy-consumption/).
This should be taken into consideration as well as it is of general importance for our society and the image of Ethereum.
From this perspective, I find the offer to buy the mining hardware much better than continuing PoW for months or years.

excerpts.author: sky.cactus
excerpts.content:
<@273808422753796097> The way I think about it is that miners have "something at stake" right now because they have hardware that is worth $X per operational time without Ethereum PoW mining and it is worth $Y per operational time with Ethereum PoW mining where `Y ~= 4X` right now.  At the moment, their hardware's value amortized over its life is `(x + y) * lifespan`.  One block before the merge, it is worth `x * lifespan + 2eth * share_of_hashing_power`.

This means that one block before the merge they effectively have epsilon "stake" in Ethereum's long term success.  Right now a miner with a 4 year amortization on hardware has something like `(2eth * 16,000,000blocks * share_of_hashing_power - y) * lifespan` (caveats here for PoS launch coming before their hardware reaches end of life) at stake in the future success of Ethereum.

excerpts.author: sky.cactus
excerpts.content: Of important note here is that `32,000,000 ETH` is substantially greater than `2 ETH`.  🙂

excerpts.author: sky.cactus
excerpts.content: So miners *will* mine right up to the last minute, but they have no reason to *not* collude to attack Ethereum, or rent their hashing power out to someone who they *know* is going to attack Ethereum.  Right now they have 32M ETH worth of reason to *not* collude with an attacker in a way that will damage Ethereum's future value.
